Hi Katie 26 Adam,

Thanks for the clear constraints. Ill summarize tradeoffs below and attach a short draft that maps each option to your constraints. TL;DR: PrivateLink gives the strongest logical isolation and least blast radius for a multi-tenant hosted model, but has higher per-interface operational cost and can complicate cross-AZ routing. VPC peering is simplest for low-latency regional traffic but scales poorly for many tenant VPCs and exposes the full route table unless you layer segmentation. A site-to-site VPN (or managed S2S with GRE/IPSec) is easiest to integrate with existing on-prem infra and can be cost-effective for bursty traffic but typically has higher and less predictable latency.

Quick matrix (high level):
- Isolation: PrivateLink > S2S VPN > Peering (unless you use dedicated VPCs per tenant)
- Predictable low latency: Peering > PrivateLink (if endpoint placement is careful) > VPN
- Operational overhead: Peering (low for few VPCs) < PrivateLink (medium) < VPN (high if you manage tunnels)
- Unit cost: varies (PrivateLink per ENI + data, Peering has no per-packet charge but cross-account costs, VPN has managed tunnel costs)

Ive attached a 2-page draft (connectivity-draft.pdf) and some quick latency numbers (latency-benchmark.csv) from a similar pilot. Ben and Kimberly, could you add any infra-specific caveats (routing limits, ENI quotas, Transit Gateway options) in replies?

Proposed next step: quick 30-min call with infra (Redwood) + BlueHarbor infra to validate preferred pattern.

Best,

Marcus 26 team,

Quick technical caveats from our infra playbook:
- VPC peering: Route table explosion is real once you have >10 tenant VPCs. Also, peering does not support transitive routing so you end up with N^2 peers for many-to-many. For sub-50ms within us-west-2 it's usually fine; watch CIDR overlap and ensure no route propagation loops.

- PrivateLink: Interface endpoints rely on ENIs in the service VPC; in heavy multitenant deployments we recommend a dedicated service VPC per region with autoscaling endpoint fleet. ENI limits per AZ can surface — require quotas or use multiple subnets. PrivateLink preserves client IP only if you proxy it (NLB + proxy layer) — without that you might lose original source IP semantics for logging.

- VPN / Managed tunnel: If you go with S2S, prefer AWS-managed VPN or a cloud VPN concentrator (e.g., a managed virtual appliance) over per-VM tunnels. Be explicit about MTU tuning (fragmentation is a frequent cause of inference QoS problems). Expect jitter that may complicate tail latency.

Other option to consider: Transit Gateway or a managed transit (AWS TGW + inter-region attachments) — combines scale with central control but adds an operational layer and costs. For strict tenant isolation weve implemented TGW with route tables per-attachment and VPC associations to simulate PrivateLink-like isolation while keeping lower latency.

Ive uploaded a short decision memo (decision-summary.md) with estimated costs and quota checklist.

Cheers,
Ben
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Katie / Adam,

Thanks for the quick responses and the helpful context. To be pragmatic for the Q3 pilot I recommend the following phased approach:

1) Pilot (4-6 weeks): PrivateLink-backed service VPC in us-west-2 with 2 ENI-backed interface endpoints. Rationale: isolates tenant traffic logically, reduces blast radius during initial onboarding, and keeps our service control plane separate. Well request ENI quota increases up-front and place endpoints across AZs to avoid single-AZ dependency.

2) Scale (post-pilot): If we see large numbers of tenant VPCs and cross-tenant mesh needs, evaluate Transit Gateway with route table isolation. TGW gives better operational scale than N^2 peering and avoids per-interface cost growth.

3) Fall-through / on-prem: For customers who must or prefer on-prem tunnels, offer a managed S2S VPN option with clear SLA on latency and jitter; use BGP + ECMP where available.
